transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Liu (Redwood SE), Elena Rodriguez (BlueHarbor Dir ML Ops), Tom Sweeney (BlueHarbor Platform), Priya Nair (BlueHarbor Security)

Summary:
BlueHarbor is evaluating Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted for inference of their real-time recommendation models. Main concerns: tenant isolation, burst readiness for Black Friday-like events, prewarm/hot-pool cost tradeoffs, and compliance (KMS/SOC2). They want a pilot in Q4 to validate latency and cost with their 7B and 70B family models.

Topics:
- Reserved GPU sizing and isolation options
- Burst routing and fallback to hosted model variants
- KV/prefix caching behavior and warm pool strategies
- Security & audit requirements (KMS, SAML, SOC2)
- Success criteria & timeline for pilot

Action items (captured above): Sophie to send pricing and prewarm playbook; Marcus to run benchmarks; Elena to share traffic profile.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to about 45, 50 minutes, lots to cover — Marcus and I are from Redwood, and you are?
[00:07] Elena: Hey Sophie, Elena here, director of ML ops at BlueHarbor. With me is Tom from Platform and Priya from Security.
[00:12] Tom: Hi all.
[00:14] Marcus: Great. Quick agenda: reserved capacity sizing, isolation needs, burst and fallback, security checklist. Sound right?
[00:20] Priya: Yes. We also want to cover audit logs and key management.
[00:24] Sophie: Perfect. To start, can you describe expected peak characteristics?
[00:29] Elena: Sure. So baseline is roughly 80 RPS for our 7B model across region A, spikes up to 1,200 RPS during promo windows, bursts are usually tens of minutes. We do multimodal calls sometimes, but predominantly text. Latency target is sub 200ms tail for simple completions, more complex reranks can be slower. We're cost sensitive — we can't justify double the token cost for long idle periods.
[00:45] Marcus: Okay, couple quick clarifiers — when you say spikes of 1,200 RPS is that sustained for 10s of minutes or hours?
[00:51] Elena: Usually 20–40 minutes, maybe a few hours at most for major launches. The distribution is very spiky, rest of month is low.
[00:58] Marcus: Got it. So two approaches: larger reserved pool to cover spikes, or smaller reserved + burst to hosted or prewarmed ephemeral GPUs. How strict are your isolation requirements?
[01:06] Tom: We need tenant fencing for customer data but model weights are not PII. For compliance reasons, we prefer compute isolation for the production tenant. So dedicated nodes or dedicated cluster.
[01:16] Priya: And we must ensure keys never leave our control — KMS integration and HSM compatibility. Also SSO + RBAC enforced for console and API keys.
[01:24] Sophie: Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem and customer-managed KMS, but for Dedicated we provide a private tenant in our infra with data-plane isolation. Marcus, can you talk tradeoffs?
[01:31] Marcus: Yeah, sure. Dedicated gives you node-level isolation and predictable throughput. You get prewarm pools — hot pools — to keep KV caches and relevant kernels warm. Cost tradeoff: hot pools consume GPU hours even idle. The other option is smaller reserved footprint and configured burst policy that routes overflow to Redwood Hosted; or fallback to smaller quantized model variants for lower cost during spikes.
[01:52] Elena: Fallback to hosted raises our data residency/e2e encryption concerns, that's why we're cautious. Is hosted encrypted in transit and at rest? How do you handle logs?
[02:02] Sophie: Hosted is TLS in transit, at-rest encryption on our side, and we support customer-managed KMS for Private; for Hosted we have audit logs and can provide SOC2 docs. For sensitive tenants we recommend Dedicated or Private. Marcus: Hosted fallback can be configured to strip user-identifiable metadata from requests, and we can route to a compatible open model that you approve. But we understand that's not always acceptable.
[02:25] Tom: Okay. For the pilot we want to try Dedicated in region A with a reserve sized to cover 60% of your observed peak, plus a burst strategy. We want clear numbers on cold-starts and how long prewarm takes.
[02:37] Marcus: Typical prewarm to reach steady KV hit rates is 5–12 minutes depending on sequence length and model. For 7B with continuous prefix caching, you can get useful hit-rates in 3–5 minutes if you warm hot pool with synthetic traffic that mirrors your distribution. Larger models like 70B can take longer and need more memory residency — prewarming can be 10–20 minutes.
[02:57] Priya: Can you quantify costs? If we keep a 2-GPU hot pool idling for the month what are the rough numbers?
[03:04] Sophie: We'll send a tailored cost sheet, but high-level: reserved GPUs are contracted monthly; an idle warm pool cost is typically the same as reserved compute units. Many customers use a mixed strategy: small warm pool for critical low-latency paths, burst to hosted for non-sensitive traffic. We'll include sample models in the playbook.
[03:22] Elena: Another concern is cache warming — if we prewarm with synthetic queries are there any privacy implications? We don't want real user data seeded into caches.
[03:31] Marcus: Synthetic traffic is recommended; you can generate anonymized prefixes. Redwood's KV cache supports TTLs and eviction policies so you can control residency. Also you can seed from model deterministic prompts that don't include real PII.
[03:44] Tom: How does autoscaling work in Dedicated? Do you spin new GPUs live or queue? We need to avoid request queuing beyond 200ms ideally.
[03:53] Marcus: Auto-scaling involves spinning up additional nodes which takes time — warm-up for a cold machine is minutes. That's why warm pools exist: they keep a small set of GPUs ready to take traffic within tens of seconds. For sudden jumps beyond warm pool capacity we recommend overflow routing to hosted or use model quantization to reduce per-token time. You can also configure pre-allocated burst credits for short spikes.
[04:16] Elena: If we route overflow to hosted, what governance controls do we have? Must be explicit approvals per route.
[04:22] Sophie: Yes. Routing policies are configurable at the customer level. You can define policies by endpoint, route, or tag, and set allowed fallback targets (hosted, quantized variant, or deny). You also get telemetry for each decision.
[04:32] Priya: Let's talk compliance: we need full audit logs for any dev or admin actions, SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning. Are those available on Dedicated?
[04:39] Marcus: Yes, Dedicated supports SAML SSO, SCIM, RBAC mapping, and audit logs. For higher control we recommend Redwood Private. We'll include export formats for logs and retention policies.
[04:49] Elena: For pilot success criteria: 99th percentile latency under 250ms for 7B, cost per 1M tokens under our target (we'll provide), and no data egress outside region. Does Dedicated support region pins?
[05:02] Sophie: Yes, you can pin to region and set routing to avoid cross-region fallback.
[05:06] Tom: We might want to try a hybrid pilot: Dedicated for critical routes, Hosted for low-sensitivity batch reranks. Can Redwood handle that mixed model routing easily?
[05:15] Marcus: Absolutely. We can route at the route/path level and provide observability per route. You'll see token-level cost and latency breakdowns in the console.
[05:22] Elena: One more technical — how do you handle KV cache replication across nodes for failover? If a node dies mid-session will we see cold starts?
[05:31] Marcus: KV cache is node-local for performance; we replicate key artifacts to durable store for faster rebuilds, but not full hot replication because of memory cost. In failover we rely on fallback model variants or warm pool warmers to reduce cold-start pain. We can tailor prewarm heartbeat strategies to your expected session patterns.
[05:49] Priya: Are there SLA guarantees on latency or only uptime?
[05:53] Sophie: Our standard SLA focuses on availability (99.9 for Dedicated), but we provide latency SLO guidance and can negotiate latency-backed terms at enterprise tier if needed.
[06:03] Tom: For benchmarking, we want to run our 7B model with our tokenization and prompts. Marcus, what do you need?
[06:10] Marcus: We'll need a containerized model artifact or model weights + tokenizer; sample input prompts and a traffic profile. Preferably a Docker tarball or an S3 link. We can run on our infra in a non-prod sandbox.
[06:21] Elena: Okay we'll prepare that. Also want to see KV hit-rates and breakdown of time in kernel vs queuing.
[06:28] Marcus: We'll surface those metrics. Expect kernel time to dominate for heavy attention. We'll also show how quantization impacts perf and memory.
[06:36] Sophie: Timeline check — you're aiming for pilot in Q4?
[06:38] Elena: Yes, ideally mid-October. We need cost/architecture review and a security review before sign-off.
[06:44] Sophie: Sounds reasonable. We'll deliver pricing and playbook by end of week, Marcus will propose benchmark slots.
[06:50] Tom: On the security review, Priya will want to see key rotation, KMS diagrams, and audit export capability.
[06:56] Priya: Also pen-test requirements and any data residency certifications.
[07:00] Marcus: We'll attach SOC2 docs and a tech note on KMS and keyflow. For pen-tests we have a process; if you need additional attestation we can coordinate with our security team.
[07:11] (brief cross-talk)
[07:15] Elena: Regarding cost, can you show a scenario where we reserve enough to cover 40% of peak and use hosted burst for the rest, versus 80% reserved? We're trying to see the unit economics.
[07:25] Sophie: We'll include a 3-scenario cost sheet: conservative (80% reserved), balanced (40% reserved + hosted burst), and minimal-reserve (20% + aggressive hosted fallback). We'll show expected monthly spend and p50/p95 latency estimates per scenario.
[07:40] Marcus: Small note — for heavy burstiness customers often choose balanced; but it's workload dependent. If your bursts are predictable within a 30-40 minute window you can prewarm before expected promotions.
[07:52] Tom: Can Redwood integrate with our deployment CI to trigger prewarm calls before product events?
[07:57] Marcus: Yes, you can call an API to seed warm pools or set a schedule in the console. We'll hand over API docs.
[08:03] Sophie: Any blockers on data residency or legal?
[08:06] Priya: We need a DPA with region constraints and explicit mention of audit log exports. Also want to ensure developer access keys are separated per environment.
[08:15] Sophie: Understood — we'll send a draft DPA and separate dev/prod key guidance.
[08:20] Elena: For the deep technical session can we carve out 90 minutes to run through benchmark results and network topology?
[08:25] Marcus: Yes, we'll book 90 mins for the SE-led deep dive. Proposed date in next bullet.
[08:30] Sophie: I'll propose 2026-09-22 10am PT for the technical deep dive.
[08:35] Elena: Works for us.
[08:37] (silence)
[08:40] Tom: A small question: how do you measure request-level cost for embeddings vs generation in the console? We want per-route token cost allocation.
[08:48] Sophie: Console shows per-route token breakdown and you can tag routes. It also shows per-model cost and per-token cost by model variant and quantization level.
[08:55] Priya: Lastly, are there limits to software versions on Dedicated? For instance, we use a custom CUDA kernel set internally.
[09:03] Marcus: Dedicated supports curated runtime versions; for Private/on-prem we can accommodate custom kernel builds with a compatibility review. For Dedicated we maintain supported stacks but can prioritize a runtime if there's a strong need. We'll document supported CUDA/cuDNN/kernel versions for your infra team.
[09:22] Elena: Great. Thanks everyone, this is helpful. Recap: Sophie to send pricing + playbook, Marcus to run benchmarks once we hand artifacts, Elena to share traffic profile. Set deep dive for 9/22.
[09:34] Sophie: Yup, I'll follow up with calendar invites and links to SOC2 and DPA drafts.
[09:39] Marcus: I'll schedule benchmark runs and share a spreadsheet to capture metrics.
[09:43] (end of meeting)
